title: To an Old Poet in Peru
text:
Because we met at evening

beneath the shadow of the station clock,

while my shadow was dying in Lima

and your ghost was dying in Lima,

old face needing a shave,

and my young beard leaping,

magnificent as dead hair

on the sands of Chancay,

because I mistakenly thought you were melancholy,

saluting your sixty years of height,

that smell of death,

of spiders on the pavement,

and you saluted my eyes

with your reedy voice,

mistakenly thinking I was great

for a young man

(my rock and roll is the movement of an angel

flying through the modern city)

(your Dark agitation is the movement

of a seraph who has lost its wings)

I kiss your fat cheek (once tomorrow

beneath the splendid Desaguadero clock)

before I go to my death in a plane crash

in North America (long ago)

and you go to your heart attack on an indifferent

street in South America)

both surrounded by shrieking Communists

with flowers in their asses,

you long before me,

or only in a long night in a room

of the old hotel of the world,

watching a black door

surrounded by paper butterflies.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Ginsberg, not recovered from the original English. The source’s “una vez mañana” is retained through the deliberately odd “once tomorrow.”

title: Celestial Words
text:
Dawn dazzles the eye

Sirens tear the sky

Taxi horns resound in the street

Broken car horns bleat bleat bleat


The sky is covered with words

The day is covered with words

The night is covered with words

God is covered with words


Consciousness covered with words

Mind covered with words

Life and death are words

Words are covered with words


Lovers are covered with words

Murderers are covered with words

Spies are covered with words

Governments covered with words


Mustard gas covered with words

Hydrogen bombs covered with words

“News” of the world is words

Wars are covered with words


Secret police covered with words

Hunger covered with words

Mothers’ bones covered with words

Skeletal children made of words


Armies are covered with words

Money covered with words

High Finance covered with words

Jungles of poverty covered with words


Electric chairs covered with words

The shouting crowd is covered with words

Tyrant radios covered with words

Televised Hell, covered with words
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Ginsberg, not recovered from the original English; the incantatory repetition and catalog structure are preserved.

title: Diamond Bells
text:
When I hear the glitter of the empty bells vibrate I realize

that Napoleon had toes

Frankenstein a big toe

Hayagriva, cosmic horse, a split big toe

The Virgin Mary, white feet, married Joseph, brown feet; a transparent white dove inseminated her

with three toes


How many toes does God have? No one knows Yahweh’s feet

or Allah’s? Muhammad, prophetic ten

Jesus Christ certainly kissed human toes


Sealo, the Seal Boy, who had flipper-hands on his shoulders

with two fingers could smoke and type with all ten toes

he sold little white deodorizers wrapped in toilet paper, one-dollar souvenirs


Shelley, ten pure pale fingers

Michelangelo had five digits per foot, Da Vinci drew ten across his two feet


The flies’ toes remain stuck to spiderwebs

spiders slide their swift feet along sticky webs

they sting the soles, the toes curl


One dark Friday night I struck the fourth toe of my bare foot against the little stair

but it still moves

walking through mud with snow is hard, it hurts the back


John Madison has chocolate toes

Hitler natural toes

Buddha, ten enlightened toes on his bare feet


To rest my skull on night pillows,

to rest in Tara’s lap among her soft toes


Lama Yab Yum dreams of twenty toes

Billions of innumerable toes, empty


When men grow old, their toenails become hard as ivory

cenotaphs grow dead nails

Napoleon wore toenails inside his well-polished boots

the elephant’s toenails strike the elbows of plants


So vibrantly does the glitter of the empty bells sound
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Ginsberg, not recovered from the original English. The source includes surreal fragments such as “billions of innumerable fingers”; these are retained without explanatory repair.

title: Sadness
text:
Give me back, he said, to the fortunate shore

where Naples reflects in a blue sea

its palaces, its slopes, its cloudless stars,

where the orange tree blooms beneath an ever-pure sky.

What is taking so long? Let us go! I still want to see again

Vesuvius burning, rising from the breast of the waters;

I want, from its heights, to see the dawn rise;

I want, guiding the one I adore,

to descend again, dreaming, from these smiling slopes;


I am on the curves of this tranquil gulf;

let us return along these shores to our familiar steps,

to Cynthia’s gardens, to Virgil’s tomb,

near the scattered fragments of Venus’s temple:


There, beneath the orange trees, beneath the flowering vine,

whose supple tendril twines with the myrtle,

and weaves a vault of flowers above your head,

to the sweet sound of the wave or murmuring wind,


with only our love, with only nature,

life and light will have more sweetness.


The torch of my past days is consumed,

gradually extinguished by the breath of misfortune,

or, if at times it casts a faint light,

it is when your memory rekindles it in my breast;


I do not know whether the gods will finally allow me

to finish my painful day here below.


My horizon is limited, and my uncertain eye

dares to extend it scarcely beyond a year.


But if I must perish in the morning,

if I must, upon a land destined for happiness,

let this cup escape my hand

that destiny seemed to hold out to me crowned with roses,


I ask the gods only to guide my steps

to the shores your beloved memory beautifies,

to greet these fortunate climates from afar,

and to die in the places where I tasted life.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Lamartine, not recovered from the French original. The source has visibly broken punctuation and line joins; the translation restores only evident sentence boundaries.

title: The Door
text:
Through that door she fled saying: “Never!”
Through that door she must return one day…
When she closed that door she left cut short
the golden thread of my hope.
Through that door she must return one day.


Each time the impulse of the breeze,
like a weak, undecided hand,
lightly shakes the window,
my coward heart awaiting her
beats faster, faster.


From my worktable I see
the door my desires dream of
and my desire lurks crouched
in the trembling depth of my eyes.


For how long, solitary, elusive,
must I wait with uncertain gaze
for God, compassionate, to return to me
the woman who fled through that door?


When will those panes tremble,
pushed by her ducal hands,
and with her kiss arrive to them,
as in winter nights there comes to me
the pious kiss of a star?
O Lord, the pale one is already alert!
O Lord, evening falls now on my road
and my dead hope freezes!
O Lord, make the door open at last
and let my beloved enter through it!…
Through that door she must return one day!
editorial_note: This is a source variant of the previously reviewed “Through That Door” poem; the English wording is kept consistent with that earlier translation.

title: Incoherences
text:
I had an ideal—where is it?

I harbored a virtue—why has it gone?

I was a Templar—where is my sturdy mail?

On what bloodied field of battle

did they leave me, sad and defeated?


O Progress, you are light! Why does your radiance

not fill my conscience? I am afraid

of the terrible doubt that poisons,

and you watch me roll upon the sand

and, like a grim vestal, lower your finger!


O decadent century, you who boast

of possessing truth, you who pride yourself

on making pacts with God and death,

give me back my faith; I am a Chactas

caressing the corpse of his Atala...


I loved, and you told me: “Analyze,”

and my passion died; I fought fiercely,

with Jesus as armor, piece by piece,

against the penetrating edge of your steel.


I thirst to know and you do not teach me;

I thirst to advance and you do not help me;

I thirst to believe and you hurl me

into the sea of theories where you dream

of finding solutions to your doubts!


And I fall, you see, and can no longer

fight without love, without serene faith

to light my path, and I am afraid...

Receive me, for God’s sake! Raise your finger,

vestal, lest they kill me in the arena!
editorial_note: The translation retains the poem’s formal address to Progress and its allusions to Chactas, Atala, and the Templar, preserving the paradox of knowledge as both light and abandonment.

title: Gratia Plena
text:
Everything about her enchanted, everything about her attracted:

her gaze, her gesture, her smile, her walk...

The wit of France flowed from her mouth.

She was “full of grace,” like the Hail Mary;

whoever saw her could never forget her!


Innocent as water, clear as day,

blond and snowy as peerless Margaret,

at the influence of her celestial soul the dawn appeared...

She was full of grace, like the Hail Mary;

whoever saw her could never forget her!


A certain sweet and gracious dignity clothed her

in I know not what distant and singular prestige.

More than many princesses, she seemed a princess:

she was full of grace, like the Hail Mary;

whoever saw her could never forget her!


I had the privilege of meeting her on my dolorous path;

through her my longing came to an end,

and my poetry found arcane cadences.

She was full of grace, like the Hail Mary;

whoever saw her could never forget her!


How, how I loved her! For ten years she was mine;

but flowers so beautiful can never last!

She was full of grace, like the Hail Mary,

and to the Fountain of Grace from which she came,

she returned... like a drop returning to the sea!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the Marian refrain and the poem’s final return of the beloved to the Fountain of Grace.

title: Requiem
text:
O Lord! God of hosts,

eternal Father, eternal King,

for this world you created

through the virtue of your power;

because you said: let there be light,

and at your word there was light;

because you coexist with the Word,

because with you the Word is

from age to age

and without tomorrow and without yesterday,


requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine,


et lux perpetua luceat eis!


O Jesus Christ, for the cold

of your Bethlehem manger,

for your anguish in the Garden,

for the vinegar and the gall,

for the thorns and the rods

with which I tore your flesh,

and for the cross on which you erased

all the sins of Israel;

Son of Man, desolate,

tragic God, terrible Judge:


requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine,


et lux perpetua luceat eis!


Divine Spirit, Paraclete,

breath of great Yahweh,

who joins Father to Son,

and being One, you are Three;

for the white-winged dove,

for the inviolate virginity

of that Virgin who in her womb

carried the Messiah Emmanuel;

for the burning red tongues

with which you inspired knowledge and faith

in the beloved disciples

of Jesus Christ, our good:


requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine,


et lux perpetua luceat eis!
editorial_note: The Latin liturgical refrain is retained; the Spanish rendering’s “con que tus carnes desgarré” remains in the first-person voice supplied by the source.

title: The Day You Love Me Will Have More Light Than June
text:
The day you love me will have more light than June;

the night you love me will be full moon,

with Beethoven notes vibrating in every ray,

its ineffable things,

and there will be more roses together

than in the whole month of May.


The crystal-clear fountains

will run along the slopes,

leaping crystal-clear

on the day you love me.


The day you love me, the hidden groves

will resound with arpeggios never heard before.

The ecstasy of your eyes: all the springtimes

that have been and will be in the world will be there when you love me.


Holding hands like fair-haired little sisters,

wearing candid collars, the daisies will go

through mountains and meadows,

before your steps, on the day you love me...

And if you pluck one, its innocent

last white petal will tell you: Passionately!


At the breaking of dawn on the day you love me,

all the clovers will have four prophetic leaves,

and in the pond, nest of unknown germs,

the mystic corollas of the lotuses will bloom.


The day you love me, every cloudbank

will be a marvelous wing; every flush of dawn, a mirage

from the Thousand and One Nights; every breeze a song,

every tree a lyre, every mountain an altar.


The day you love me, for the two of us

the beatitude of God will fit inside a single kiss.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the conditional future, botanical imagery, and the final compression of divine beatitude into one kiss.

title: Rubén Darío Has Died...
text:
Rubén Darío has died,

the one of precious stones!


Brother, how many nights your spirit and mine,

joined for flight like two eager wings,

wanted to sound the dark Enigma hungrily,

beyond the stars and the nebulae!


Rubén Darío has died,

the one of precious stones!


How many intense years we lived beside the Seine,

setting our youthful verses

in the gold of a common ideal,

which sometimes we saw spring

like two roses blooming at once from a rosebush!


Today your restless life, like a wild torrent,

has emptied into the Sea of Causes; now you rest

your wandering feet on the cold islet

painted by Böcklin... now you know all things!


Rubén Darío has died,

the one of precious stones!


My belated waves follow yours; but soon,

in the unfathomable and eternal sea of everything,

my spirit will be sated with what I wish to know:

the How and the Why, Essence and Mode.


And you, as in Lutetia on those mysterious afternoons

when we thought together beside the lyrical River,

will have to guide me... I will go where you dare,

to steal together from the musical void

and from the choir of the orbs their portentous keys...


Rubén Darío has died,

the one of precious stones!
editorial_note: The translation keeps Nervo’s repeated elegy refrain and the shared astronomical and musical metaphors for Darío’s death.

title: Bonsoir
text:
Good night, my love, and until tomorrow!

Until tomorrow, yes, when dawn breaks,

and I, after forty years

of incoherent dreaming, open and rub

the eyes of the spirit,

like one who has slept a very, very long time,

and slowly begins to awaken,

and, in a progressive lucidity,

ties the threads of yesterday in my soul

(before the flesh bound it)

to the prodigious today

in which I shall find myself, on this plane

where nothing is illusion and everything

is truth...


Good night, my love,

good night! I remain in darkness

and you flew toward dawn...

Until tomorrow, love, until tomorrow!


For even if destiny

were to pile five-year spans upon five-year spans

of my lifelong imprisonment, those spans

are fleeting; the days follow one another

like rosaries whose great beads

are Sundays...


They are Sundays on which, with my flowers,

I go unfailingly to the cemetery

where your beloved forms lie.

How many bouquets of flowers

have I carried to the grave? I do not know.

How many must I carry? Perhaps only a few now.

Perhaps only a few! Oh, what a delightful prospect!


Perhaps the jailer

is approaching with his ringing keys

to open my cell forever!

Is it perhaps the echo of his steps

that can be heard, moving through the quiet corridors

beyond the window?


Good night, love of my loves!

Until later, perhaps... or until tomorrow.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the address “Bonsoir,” the prison-and-cemetery imagery, and the speaker’s ambiguous hope for release.

title: I Loved the Blue Ardently
text:
I loved the blue ardently:

the exalted mountains, the subtle

sapphire crêpes of the firmament,

the endless sea, whose lament

cradled my youthful dreams.


My lute fell silent when each pure star

unfurled its bud,

the universe sailed in stillness,

and the moon, a silver sickle, rose and reaped

the sheaf of the night’s thick shadows.


I sang when dawn drew back

its rosy veils in the East,

when the dew descended upon the fields,

and the sun, a golden urn opening,

flooded all the heavens with light.


But today I love the night, the graceful one,

of sweet majesty, tranquil

and solemn hours, the sovereign Nubian,

the one of splendid American pomp:

the tropical night of your pupils!


Today I evade the blushes of dawn;

its golden arrow wounds me,

and the heart, without sorrow or anger,

dilates only before the blackness of your eyes,

like the iris of an owl.


What enchantment could equal yours,

O my night? Your beauty astonishes me!

I, who flee the splendors of morning,

let my soul flutter, like a firefly,

its sparkling wings in your shadow!


If I must always feel that gaze

fixed upon my face, powerful and tender,

farewell forever, blond dawn!

maiden in rose-colored dress:

may eternal night reign around me!


O night! Come to me, full of enchantment;

while you advance on mysterious wings,

my song will be for you alone,

and in the brown folds of your mantle,

my hopes will open their cups!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s conversion from daylight to the beloved’s tropical night, including the moon’s sickle, owl’s iris, and firefly imagery.

title: The Woman Who in My Blooming...
text:
The woman who in my blooming

youth could have been

—if God had wished—

mine,


in the inner landscape

of a paradise of love

and poetry;


the one who, noblewoman or peasant,

“my peasant” or “my princess,”

would have been called,

is, in my book, Damiana.


The laughing, holy daughter,

twin of seraphim,

perhaps a dragonfly in my gardens

and an infanta in my realm;


the one who

could give faith to the soul,

vigor to effort, good sense

to action—the one who did not come,

no matter how much I called her!


The one who still kisses my brow

from a distant star,

that one

is, in my book, Damiana.


And the one who looked at me,

I do not know in what beloved homeland,

after looking at me passed on

(this was more than a lifetime ago);


and as she looked at me she seemed

to be saying:

“If I could stop,

I would love you”...


the one who repeated this to me with her eyes;

the one whom, seated at the table

of the royal feast, I awaited

with vain unease, that one

is, in my book, Damiana;


The one who, with noble bearing,

usually wanders fluidly

like a lunar ghost

through the region of my dream;


the one who gleams in sunsets,

which are the day’s nobility,

the one who in the melancholy

of my room feigns footsteps,


the one whom, posted at the window,

with an unceasing longing,

I have awaited for a century,

that one is, in my book, Damiana.


Everything noble and beautiful

that did not come to be;

everything lovely and kind

that did not arrive;


and the vague and mysterious

things I thought,

and the pure and ineffable

and divine;


the enigma always clear in the morning

and the enigma unspoken in the afternoon;

love, dreams, ideal, arcane essence,

all that, all that, all that,

has a name in these pages: Damiana!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the poem’s catalog of unrealized women and its recurring identification of them all as Damiana.

title: Sleep
text:
What I have, my friend, is a profound

desire to sleep!... You know? Sleep

is a state of divinity.

The one who sleeps is a god... What I have,

my friend, is a great desire to sleep.


Sleep is in life our only world,

for wakefulness immerses us

in the common illusion, in the ocean

of so-called “Reality.” Awake

we all see the same thing:

we see earth, water, air, fire,

ephemeral creatures... Asleep,

each person is in their world,

in their exclusive world:

hermetic, closed to alien eyes,

to alien souls; each mind spins

its own dream (or its truth: who knows?)


Not even the most adored being

can enter with us through the door

of our sleep. Not even the wife

who shares your bed

and hears you converse with the phantoms

that cross your spirit

while you sleep could,

even if she longed to,

cross the thresholds of that world,

your wondrous world of shadows.


O blessed are those who sleep!

For them each night the universe

that our spirit creates each day

is extinguished with all its pain.

When they put out its light, the cosmos goes out.


The greatest punishment is wakefulness:

insomnia is exile

from the best paradise...


No one, not even the happiest, would want

to subtract hours from sleep to be happy.

Not even the beloved woman

is worth a gentle, serene sleep

in the arms of Him who suggests

holy inspirations...

“The day belongs to men; but the night

belongs to the gods,” the ancients said.


Do not disturb my peace, then, with your speeches,

friend: you know much;

but my sleep knows more... Go away!

I want neither glory nor inheritance:

what I have, my friend, is a profound

desire to sleep...
editorial_note: The translation preserves Nervo’s metaphysics of sleep as a private world and the final contrast between human day and divine night.

title: On the Road
text:
I


He Resolves to Return to the Father


Do not fear, Christ the King, if I set out astray

after mad ideals:

neither in my days of tears have I forgotten you,

nor in my hours of happiness have I forgotten you.


In the cruel wound in your side

the soul wishes to form its nest,

forgetting the dreams it has lived

and the sad lies it has dreamed.


In the light of pain, which already shows me

my world of phantoms turned to rubble,

I will go to the foot of your mystical mountain,


with tedium as a staff in my left hand;

with purple rags upon my shoulders,

with a bundle of chimeras on my back.


II


How They Will Rejoice at His Return


I will return like the suffering Prodigal

to your tranquil estate; I can no longer

tend the herd, and I fear

the pitiless brightness of the suns.


You will come out diligently to meet me;

I will tell you quietly, very quietly, of my illness...

and you will leave a kiss upon my brow

and a wedding ring upon my finger;


and gathering around the hearth

the old friends of the neighborhood,

while they eat merrily at your table,


you will cry out in profound rejoicing:

“Rejoice in my happiness, for the son

whom we mourned as lost is returning!”


III


He Weighs the Intensity of the Life to Come


Oh yes, I will return; your love presses

with invincible urgency upon the thought,

which hungers for peace and solitude

in the gentle quiet of the charterhouse.


Oh yes, I will return; already outlined

in the depths of the soul, I sense

the peaceful silhouette of the convent

with its white dome and graceful spire...


There, finally alone with myself,

hearing in Isaiah’s voices

your insinuating cry that calls my name,


how I will drown myself in silence,

how I will lose myself in the cloisters,

how I will merge with the shadow!
editorial_note: The translation preserves the three-part devotional sequence, its Prodigal Son imagery, and the return from wandering to a charterhouse.

title: The Marquis de Sade
text:
The Marquis de Sade has reentered the erupting volcano

from which he had emerged,

with his beautiful hands still adorned with fringes,

his maiden’s eyes,

and that permanent reasoning of every-man-for-himself

so exclusively his.


But from the phosphorescent salon lit by lamps of entrails

he has never ceased to issue mysterious commands

that open a breach in the moral night.


Through that breach I see

the great creaking shadows, the old worn crust,

fading away

to let me love you

as the first man loved the first woman,

with complete freedom.


That freedom

through which fire itself has become man,

through which the Marquis de Sade defied the centuries

with his great abstract trees

and tragic acrobats

clinging to the thread of the Virgin of desire.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Breton, not recovered from the French original; the surreal syntax and charged images are preserved.

title: Give Me Drowned Jewels
text:
Give me the jewels of drowned women

Two mangers

A ponytail and a dressmaker’s mania

Then forgive me

I have no time to breathe

I am a destiny

The solar construction has held me until now

And now I only have to let myself die

Ask for the scale

At a trot, with a closed fist over my ringing head

A lantern in which a yellow gaze opens

Feeling opens too

But the princesses cling to pure air

I need pride

And a few common drops

To warm the cauldron of moldy flowers

At the foot of the staircase

Divine thought in the cracked glass of the blue sky

The bathers’ expression is the death of the wolf

Take me for a friend

The friend of bonfires and ferrets

It looks at you twice

It reads your sorrows

My rosewood oar makes your hair sing...
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Breton, not recovered from the French original; the fragment sequence remains intentionally unresolved.

title: An Absolutely White Man and Woman
text:
At the bottom of the parasol I see the marvelous prostitutes

with their slightly worn dress beside the forest-colored lamp.

They stroll with

a large piece of wallpaper,

like the old floors of a house being demolished

that one cannot contemplate without one’s heart tightening,

or a shell of white marble

torn from a mantelpiece,

or a net of those chains that behind them

become entangled.


The great instinct of combustion takes possession of the streets

where they remain

like roasted flowers.


Their eyes raise in the distance

a wind of stone in the mirrors,

while they plunge motionless

into the center of the whirlwind.


Nothing equals for me the meaning of their

careless thought,

the freshness of the stream in which their boots wet the shadow

of its peak,

the reality of those handfuls of cut hay in which

they disappear.


I see their breasts, which set a point of sunlight in the deep night,

where the time of bending and rising is the only

exact measure of life.


I see their breasts, stars upon waves,

their breasts

in which the invisible blue milk weeps forever.


Version by Manuel Álvarez Ortega
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering of Breton, not recovered from the French original. The translator credit in the source is retained; the source’s deliberately unstable surreal syntax is left open.

title: A Stone, Memory
text:
Where, you say, now, are those steps

through the unknown, in the

first solitude.


Latitude of the vines, far away.

The final sun opened its

remote flank

over the stones, over the leaves, in a last

dream, the end of summer.

It was dusk,

it was another land, perhaps darker,

the red earth, yes,

as if some ember of the origin

still breathed in it,

beyond, at the end of all impermanence,

as in the distance.


Arcane light,

suspension of suns over the plantains.


It was

all that certainly burned in the invisible.

It was only the light,

as if empty, and as if it could see

its dark burning

in the ferns, in the sky,

over the earth.

Then, to return from there,

over the same steps,

but now, I knew, unrepeatable.

The house

was always a thing of light.

From that day it knew the shadow, or its

sign.

There, upon a stone,

inscribed in the remote, beneath

the wounded light,

a sign for summer, the end, beside the vines,


the end that was an origin,

A., September, the suns, upon an

extreme stone.


From “White Fire,” 1992
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering; the fractured spacing and recursive memory image are preserved, with no title or source-text repair beyond evident line joining.

title: A Window onto the World
text:
For my hotel at night a sky rises

from the estuary slowly.

A bog of stars burns and this plaza

solitary, remains in

silence.

Without the sleepless lights of the tram,

without its yellow fruit and its clamor,

the steep streets fall asleep,

empty of children, and the shops

and liquor stores begin to close.

The hill is gentle and the greens are

a ruined estate, some palms,

a sad and certain colonial air,

witnesses that the Tagus reaches the

sea

and black ships with light bulbs reach the port.

Its siren is hoarse

like smoke!

Beautiful animals of the night,

funeral carriages

upon the water!

Old cities where there is always someone leaning out

over the balcony and the windows.

If I could be at that height,

I would look in silence and last forever:

all the blue, the river, and memory.

Down this street, there where I cannot reach

to see, my hotel,

the end where I look at myself

and another, in my place, leaves my name in a name

of another city and another river.


From "" 1991
editorial_note: The source’s “lentaniente” is corrected to the evident “lentamente” (“slowly”); the empty collection title in the supplied footer is retained as “From "" 1991” rather than invented.
